To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

human monocytes attached to and damaged Candida albicans pseudohyphally in vitro, and that myeloperoxide-independent and nonoxidant mechanisms could sometimes damage Candida albicans when oxidative mechanisms were impaired.

monocyte-mediated damage to Candida albican hyphae and pseudohyphae occurs by a mechanism that is dependent on myeloperoxidases and hydrogen peroxide, and that the damage to Candida hypha is greater than that to monocyte cells in vitro.
monocytes, but not neutrophils, damage hyphae of Candida albican in the absence of opsonic factors, and that the damage is predominantly myeloperoxidases dependent.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the mechanisms by which monocytes kill hyphae and pseudohyphae of Candida albicants in vitro.
the role of monocytes in host defense against Candida.
the mechanisms of damage by human monocytes to hyphal forms of the yeast Candida albicans.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
Candida albicans can be damaged by human monocytes in the absence of complement or opsonins.
oxidative mechanisms were important in damage to Candida hypha by monocytes, whereas nonoxidative mechanisms did not appear to be important.
monocytes, but not neutrophils, can damage hyphae in vitro without serum.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
oxidative mechanisms of monocytes are important for damage and killing of Candida hypha in serum-free systems.

oxidative mechanisms were important in damage to Candida albican hyphae and pseudohyphae by human peripheral blood monocytes in vitro, and that monocytes were damaged by interactions with hyphae and probably killed them.

monocytes, like neutrophils, can damage and probably kill Candida hyphaes and pseudohyphae by myeloperoxidate-independent and nonoxidant mechanisms, but oxidative mechanisms are more important for damage to Candida hypha by monocytes than they were by neutrophils.
The main takeaway from our work is that
monocytes can damage Candida hyphaes without serum, and this damage is likely mediated by oxidative mechanisms.
monocytes can damage hyphal forms of C. albicans in the absence of opsonins and serum.
monocyte damage to Candida hypha is mediated primarily by oxidative mechanisms, which are not dependent on serum.
